title: SpaceX caught a spaceship falling from orbit

scenes.narration: On Saturday, a giant steel spaceship fell back from orbit, flipped upright, and was caught in mid-air by a tower's arms. No spaceship returning from orbit had ever been caught before.
It started on Friday at Starbase, Texas. Starship, the tallest rocket ever built at 124 metres, lit 33 engines and lifted off on its 15th test flight.

The plan was a first: catch both stages. But on the way home, the Super Heavy booster detected a guidance problem and called off its catch. It diverted over the Gulf, hovered, and blew itself up just above the water.
The ship kept climbing into orbit, about 275 kilometres up, and released 26 new Starlink satellites.
Then it circled the Earth for nearly a day: about 14 orbits in 22 and a half hours, the longest Starship flight so far.
On Saturday afternoon, it came home. The ship hit the atmosphere belly first, its black heat shield glowing inside a sheath of plasma.
Over Texas it fell like a skydiver. Then, close to the tower, three engines lit, and it swung upright.
It slowed, slid between the arms, and the tower caught it by two small pins, each about a foot long. Caught. A first for any spaceship coming back from orbit.
Why does it matter? Rockets are usually thrown away after one flight. SpaceX wants a fully and rapidly reusable rocket, refuelled and flown again, like an airliner.
Next comes refuelling in orbit, one Starship filling another. NASA needs that before Starship can land astronauts on the Moon, a landing now targeted for 2028.
But it was only half a win. The booster was lost, and SpaceX has yet to catch one of its newest boosters. Next flight, the goal is both.
